archetype.name: Better Than Its Record (process-first)
archetype.definition: A Buffalo team that controls 5-on-5 play like a top-ten club but is giving the gains back through goaltending and special teams, and so sits at .500 with a negative goal differential.

report.headline: Winning the 5-on-5 chances, losing everything at the margins: goaltending and special teams
report.take:
Seven games into the season, Buffalo is two teams at once. At 5-on-5 the Sabres look like the club that won 50 games last year, and in one way better. Their 54.9% share of expected goals and 54% share of shot attempts both rank 8th, well above the even 50% xGF they posted during that 50-23-9 season. Everywhere else they look like the sub-.500 Sabres of the early 2020s. The power play converts 11.1% (29th), the penalty kill stops only 60.9% (30th), and the goalies are a combined 3.9 goals below expected (26th). Put those together and you get a 3-3-1 record, a -7 goal differential and 23rd place on the site.

The defense corps is driving the good part. Owen Power plays 26.44 minutes a night with a 61.5% xGF share and seven points. Rasmus Dahlin sits 11th on the defensemen tab, and Olen Zellweger's 65.6% xGF is the best on the roster. That B+ blueline grade reflects real play, not one player. The forwards grade a C- because the production is thin behind Tage Thompson. He has four goals on 31 shots, by far the most shots of any forward. The depth centers are mostly between 128th and 174th on their tab, and Ryan McLeod is a -5 in 15 minutes a night. The group as a whole has 12 goals on 115 shots, which says as much about cold finishing as about a lack of talent.

The numbers hide two things that pull in opposite directions. The bad news is that the record is, if anything, a little flattering. Buffalo is 1.4 points ahead of what its goal differential implies (5th), thanks to one-goal wins over Chicago and Minnesota and a loser point. The good news is that the underlying causes of that differential are the least sticky things in hockey. A 96.2 PDO, an .850 save percentage from Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen and a penalty kill failing at that rate are not what a good-process team usually sustains. Last year's team posted 24.5 goals saved above expected and a 102 PDO on an even chance share, so these goalies can be much better than this.

The direction depends on whether the crease and the kill drift back toward normal while the 5-on-5 edge holds. If both happen, this is a playoff-caliber team that started cold. If the goaltending is genuinely a D-grade group, the strong chance share only keeps it in the bubble conversation. The sample is seven games, so the honest read is that the process deserves more trust than the results.

strengths.title: Controlling play at 5-on-5
strengths.body: Buffalo ranks 8th in both expected-goal share and shot-attempt share, so it is owning territory and chances rather than hanging on. That is a step up from last year's even split. Shot-share numbers stabilize faster than finishing or save percentage, which makes this the most trustworthy thing on the sheet. It should keep generating more chances than opponents even when the bounces stay bad.

strengths.title: A blueline that drives the bus
strengths.body: Power logs heavy minutes with a 61.5% xGF share and a team-best seven points among defensemen. Dahlin ranks 11th on the defensemen tab, and Zellweger has the strongest chance share on the club. The B+ grade rests on three or four genuinely good players, not one star. That gives it staying power, though the bottom pair is under water.

strengths.title: Thompson shooting at volume
strengths.body: Thompson has four goals on 31 shots and sits 16th on the centers tab. He is the one forward turning the territorial edge into a constant threat. His shot volume is the repeatable part, and it gives the offense a floor while the rest of the forwards' finishing catches up.

concerns.title: Goaltending bleeding goals
concerns.body: Luukkonen has taken most of the work with an .850 save percentage and 3.6 goals below expected. That is most of the team's -3.9 GSAx. Colten Ellis has been roughly average in his three starts. Some recovery is almost certain at a 96.2 PDO, but a D grade over a full year would cap this team no matter how well it plays in front of the net.

concerns.title: Special teams in the basement
concerns.body: A 60.9% penalty kill and an 11.1% power play, both bottom-four, are turning a 5-on-5 edge into losing nights. In recent seasons the kill has ranged from the mid-70s to the low 80s, so the current figure is very likely noise plus poor goaltending. The power play has been mediocre for a few years and is less likely to bounce all the way back.

concerns.title: Record already gets some help
concerns.body: Despite a -7 differential, Buffalo has banked more points than its goals imply, 5th-most in the league. The two-goal-or-closer wins over Chicago and Minnesota could easily have gone the other way. If the goal differential doesn't improve, the standings will catch up with it. Opposing forwards, and wingers especially, are also piling up points far beyond their norms against this defense.

trend.note: Results have bounced between wins and losses, with no streak longer than two either way. A shutout loss to Dallas and a five-goal night against Florida came within a week of each other. The 5-on-5 numbers have been steadier than the scoreboard.

weekAhead.headline: Two road divisional tests, then the league's worst team at home
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with a pair of Atlantic road games against teams level with or just ahead of Buffalo, then a long break before Philadelphia visits. Toronto is a strange matchup. The Leafs get badly out-chanced at 5-on-5 (28th in xGF %) but survive on elite special teams and goaltending. That attacks exactly where Buffalo is weakest. Montreal is close to a mirror image of the Sabres: strong shot shares, a poor power play and below-average goaltending. The Canadiens just beat Buffalo 4-3 two days before this rematch.

Philadelphia is winless and last in both expected-goal share and shot-attempt share, and 32nd on the site. If Buffalo's 5-on-5 edge is real, that game should look lopsided. It is also the cleanest chance for the goaltending to post a quiet night. A strong week here means taking at least one in Atlantic road buildings and not giving away the Flyers game.

keyMatchups.title: Buffalo's kill vs Toronto's power play
keyMatchups.body: Toronto converts 29.2% of its power plays (5th) and kills 95.8% (1st). Buffalo sits near the bottom of the league in both. At even strength the Sabres should have the edge against a team this out-chanced, so staying out of the box may decide the game.

keyMatchups.title: Power and Dahlin against Montreal
keyMatchups.body: Montreal's defense gives up the second-most points beyond expectation to defensemen (30th), and defensemen take an unusually large share of the points against it. That plays to Buffalo's best group. Power's minutes and Dahlin's shot volume are the obvious levers in the rematch.

keyMatchups.title: Philadelphia's possession collapse
keyMatchups.body: The Flyers own just 34.5% of the expected goals and 40% of the shot attempts, both last in the league, and score the fewest goals per game. A team out-chancing opponents the way Buffalo does should control this one throughout. The bigger question is whether the shooters finally convert.

weekAhead.watch: Who gets the starts in goal. Ellis has been near average while Luukkonen has been well below, and how the crease splits this week may matter more than any skater.

restOfSeason.body:
The bet here is on the 5-on-5 numbers. Seven games is a tiny sample, but shot and chance shares settle faster than save percentage, PDO or penalty-kill rates, and all three of those are at levels that rarely last for a team that plays this well. Expect the kill to climb back toward the range of recent seasons, and expect the team save percentage to rise even if Luukkonen never matches last year's group. Together those should turn the goal differential positive. The record's small boost from close games will probably fade, so the gains have to come from real goal-differential improvement, not more one-goal wins.

The ceiling depends on the forwards beyond Thompson. A C- group with depth centers ranked deep on their tab won't carry the offense if the blueline cools. The power play has also been a weakness for years, so treat it as a likely drag rather than a coming rebound. That profile points to a team in the playoff mix, more likely near the cut line than near last year's top-five finish unless the goaltending returns to last season's level.
swingFactors: Luukkonen's save percentage returning to league-average
Secondary scoring from the depth centers

confidence.note: Seven games. Shot shares are telling, but goaltending and special-teams samples are tiny.
